newsitem.title: USA: Conf tolds half air cargo processes redundant.
newsitem.headline: Conf tolds half air cargo processes redundant.

text.p: Half or more of the processes in the traditional flow of international air cargo from shipper to consignee can be dropped, allowing freight to move considerably faster, and at less cost, cargo automation officials told IATA Cargo Week 97.

Reforming the international air cargo flow to meet the growing threat from integrated carriers like FedEx and DHL Worldwide Express was the prime focus of Cargo Week, following the formation last Sunday of Cargo 2000, a joint forwarder/airline project to point the industry towards the largest overhaul in its history.
The Cargo 2000 executive - headed by United Airlines cargo vice-president Jim Hartigan - holds its first meeting Monday in London.

As if to underscore the need for Cargo 2000, speakers at Cargo Week 97 warned that without reform, the demise of the traditional air cargo channel - comprising freight forwarders and combination (passenger/cargo) airlines - is likely to occur within a matter of years.

They described the system as hidebound, inefficient and riddled with practices which serve no purpose, a world where freight takes twice as much time, on average, as it should to reach the consignee, a world where freight can spend days on end sitting in airport or off-airport warehouses, a world slow to embrace tried and true technology like bar coding, let alone paperless EDI transactions.

Dublin-based consultant John Hartnett told the Women in Freight symposium at Cargo Week that without major reform, and fast, the combination airlines will lose most of the international freight market, and certainly all high value goods like computers, to the integrators.
Until recently, he said, the traditional carriers lived in denial about how slowly freight moved through their systems versus the streamlined networks of the integrated carrier.

Hugh Doyle, Dublin-based managing director, freight management, for Unisys Corp, told Reuters at Women in Freight that the problem does not arise from the fact that the traditional air freight system involves more players than the integrated carriers, with their door to door service. The traditional system has the potential to move freight just as quickly, he said.

Unisys conducted a survey of 2,000 international cargo shipments last year. It found that half of the 40 storage, handling and administrative functions in the average international move are useless, add cost but "absolutely zero" value, and can be dropped without any loss of service quality. In fact, everything would move a lot faster.

At Cargo Week, Unisys unveiled a flow chart for a revised airline/forwarder traffic flow. It entails only 20 functions by making increased use of scanner technology many carriers already have in place.

I would suggest that not another dollar needs to be spent much beyond our study, said Doyle. If they (forwarders and airlines) implement what we have shown here, they can achieve at least 90 percent of the benefit, and any other big investment will be to try and get incremental benefit.

Implementing these reforms need not be complicated, he said. Redundant processes can be dropped one by one, over as much as five years. Doyle said a streamlined forwarder/airline system as envisioned by Unisys should be able to move 95 percent of international freight just as fast as the integrated carriers do - an average of three days.

Unisys found that the average international shipment in its survey took six days to move through the traditional freight channel, was handled 36 times along the way, was stored in various airline or forwarder warehouses eight times and generated about 12 pieces of paper.

Half of all international shipments spend at least three days sitting in an import freight terminals, the survey found. Doyle said he will know the airlines are serious about reform when they announce that they are getting out of warehousing freight at airports.
"When that starts happening, I think the rate of change will be very quick. It's a psychological thing," he stated.
